title: Rethinking Underwater Image Enhancement: Learning through Text-Guided Degradation Curriculum

paper.title: Rethinking Underwater Image Enhancement: Learning through Text-Guided Degradation Curriculum
paper.abstract:
Abstract Existing paired clean–degraded datasets have advanced learning-based underwater image enhancement, but they remain either limited in scale or difficult to acquire, and still fail to adequately cover the diverse degradations encountered in real-world underwater environments. Such scarce and insufficient data ultimately restrict the generalization of underwater image enhancement models, highlighting the need for realistic and controllable degradation modeling to better capture real underwater conditions and improve enhancement robustness.
To this end, we propose a unified degradation-aware training framework for the underwater image enhancement task. A Text-Conditioned Degradation Augmentation Pipeline uses a text-guided diffusion model to synthesize diverse and semantically consistent degraded samples, providing paired data to support the subsequent curriculum learning strategy. The proposed Progressive Degradation Curriculum organizes training across multiple attributes and difficulty levels to promote balanced learning, and a Transmission-Guided One-Step Diffusion Model leverages this progressive process to better address the wide range of degradation severity and restoration ambiguity in underwater images.
Extensive experiments on multiple underwater benchmarks demonstrate that our proposed method achieves superior performance. Our code and models will be released upon the publication of this work.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Underwater Image Enhancement (UIE) aims to recover clear, color-consistent, and detail-preserving images from degraded underwater observations. Unlike uniform degradations in common image restoration tasks, underwater degradations are highly heterogeneous and scene-dependent, where they vary with water type, depth, illumination, and particle density, and often exhibit complex spatial coupling among these factors. Consequently, the underlying degradation distribution is extremely difficult to model or approximate with a fixed prior, making UIE an intrinsically ill-posed and data-sensitive problem. Over the past decade, a wide range of enhancement approaches have been explored, spanning from physics-based restoration guided by analytical priors Drews et al. (2013) ; Galdran et al. (2015) ; Chiang and Chen (2011) to deep learning-based methods trained on paired datasets Li et al. (2020) ; Li et al. (2021) ; Wang et al. (2021) ; Zhang et al. (2022) ; Wei et al. (2022) ; Li et al. (2019a) . While the former provides physical interpretability, it fails to generalize across diverse water types and illumination conditions. The latter achieves stronger visual quality through elaborately designed networks but relies heavily on limited paired data. Acquiring paired underwater data is inherently challenging because capturing the same scene under both degraded and clean conditions is almost impossible in dynamic environments. As illustrated in Figure 1 -Top, such pairs are commonly obtained through (i) controlled water-tank capture Duarte et al. (2016) , (ii) pseudo-reference generation by manually selecting outputs from multiple UIE methods Li et al. (2019a) ; Peng et al. (2023) , or (iii) synthetic rendering with simplified underwater formation models Islam et al. (2020) ; Li et al. (2017) ; Ye et al. (2022) ; Li et al. (2020) . The first two routes provide visually realistic supervision but are costly and difficult to scale, whereas the third enables scalable generation but often fails to reproduce the complex lighting and scattering effects of natural underwater scenes. These limitations reveal that the main bottleneck of UIE lies not only in model architecture but also in the lack of realistic and controllable degradation modeling for generating diverse training variants. Moreover, underwater degradations vary drastically in strength and composition—ranging from light color cast to dense scattering and mixed turbidity. This motivates us to rethink UIE — not as direct restoration, but as learning from degradation , where controllable, text-guided degradation modeling provides structured, degradation-aware supervision for enhancement learning. In addition, we argue that if degradations can be explicitly modeled and controlled, they can serve as a meaningful curriculum for enhancement, where the model gradually adapts to increasingly challenging degradations across multiple attributes and severity levels, which encourages more generalized enhancement performance. To this end, we revisit underwater enhancement from a new perspective-leveraging the generative capability of the diffusion model to explicitly model and control underwater degradations (Figure 1 -Medium). Diffusion-based generative models Labs et al. (2025) provide an expressive latent space in which degradations can be synthesized and conditioned on semantic cues such as turbidity, illumination, or particle density. This text-conditioned formulation enables fine-grained control over degradation attributes and supports large-scale data augmentation aligned with real underwater characteristics. The generated degradations further provide difficulty-aware cues that guide enhancement models to learn progressively under well-structured degradation distributions, yielding more stable optimization and visually coherent restoration across diverse underwater conditions. Moreover, we develop a Transmission-Guided One-Step Diffusion enhancer that injects a transmission prior into the latent space and performs a single deterministic reverse update, providing transmission-guided restoration with lower sampling cost than multi-step diffusion methods. Together, these designs establish a cohesive paradigm that unifies controllable degradation modeling and physically guided enhancement, offering a new perspective on the UIE task. Overall, our contributions can be summarized as follows: • We introduce a Text-Conditioned Degradation Augmentation (TCDA) pipeline that leverages a text-guided diffusion model to synthesize controllable degraded variants of clean images, enabling fine-grained attribute/severity control for task-aligned data augmentation. • We employ a progressive degradation curriculum learning that gradually increases training difficulty, stabilizing optimization and improving the model’s robustness. • We design a Transmission-Guided One-step Diffusion model (TG-Diff) that embeds a transmission prior into the latent space, achieving high-quality restoration with greater inference efficiency than multi-step diffusion methods. • Extensive experiments on multiple underwater benchmarks demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance. Figure 2: Overview of the proposed Text-Conditioned Degradation Augmentation (TCDA) pipeline. It consists of four stages: (1) Degradation Captioning via MLLMs for generating fine-grained textual descriptions of underwater degradations, (2) Flow-Based Degradation Modeling for learning text-conditioned mappings between clean and degraded representations, (3) Prompt-Space Augmentation for enriching degradation prompts with varying difficulty levels, and (4) Text-Conditioned Degradation Synthesis for controllable degradation generation to support curriculum learning.

sections.heading: 2.1 Underwater Image Enhancement
sections.text: Traditional UIE methods are typically built upon the underwater image formation model that characterizes light scattering and absorption. Early works such as underwater dark channel prior Drews et al. (2013) , red channel prior Galdran et al. (2015) , and blurriness-based estimation Chiang and Chen (2011) estimate the transmission map and background light to remove haze and recover true colors. More recent prior-based methods further exploit illumination characteristics to handle non-uniform lighting and color degradation Hou et al. (2023) ; Zhou et al. (2025b) . However, their performance heavily depends on accurate estimation of water parameters and scene depth, limiting their robustness across varying underwater conditions Liu et al. (2020) . Deep learning has revolutionized UIE by providing strong nonlinear modeling and robust feature representation capabilities. Early convolutional methods Li et al. (2020) ; Li et al. (2021) ; Wang et al. (2021) ; Zhang et al. (2022) ; Wei et al. (2022) employed encoder–decoder or multi-branch architectures to learn direct mappings from degraded to clean images, achieving improved contrast and color fidelity through illumination modeling and multi-level feature learning. Adversarial and generative frameworks Fabbri et al. (2018) ; Wang et al. (2019) further enhanced perceptual realism but often introduced instability and color over-saturation. Moreover, some works use contrastive learning Zhou et al. (2024) , domain priors, and external knowledge to improve UIE generalization and controllability. PhaseFormer Khan et al. (2025) introduces phase-based attention to preserve structural cues, while CLIP-UIE Liu et al. (2025) utilizes semantic guidance from vision-language models. Semantic-Guided Diffusion Zhou et al. (2025a) leverages multimodal cues from LLaVA and Zip-CLIP to generate semantic heatmaps for diffusion guidance. Recent studies highlight the role of generative priors and degradation modeling in diffusion-based image restoration Li et al. (2025) . Underwater-specific approaches, including WF-Diff Zhao et al. (2024) and SLURPP Wu et al. (2025) , exploit diffusion models for underwater enhancement. Related diffusion-based restoration methods further explore degradation-model optimization Fei et al. (2026) , global brightness alignment Guo et al. (2026) , and blur-decoupled learning Cheng et al. (2026) . Despite these advances, the effectiveness of related UIE methods remains largely constrained by the availability and diversity of training data.

sections.heading: 2.2 Underwater Image Synthesis
sections.text: The scarcity of paired and diverse underwater data has motivated the research on underwater image synthesis. Early physics-based methods simulate light attenuation using simplified water models but fail to reproduce complex scattering Ye et al. (2022) ; Li et al. (2020) . Alternatively, some datasets create pseudo-references by applying multiple UIE methods to a degraded image and having a user select the best outcome as the “clean” target Li et al. (2019a) . While visually plausible, this approach is fundamentally limited as it provides no insight into the forward degradation process itself. It merely offers a single, fixed enhancement target for each input, failing to model the diverse and controllable degradation attributes (e.g., water type, turbidity) that are crucial for robust generalization. GAN-based approaches Li et al. (2017) ; Islam et al. (2020) improve realism but suffer from domain bias and unstable training. Recent diffusion-driven frameworks, including Atlantis++ Zhang et al. (2026) and TIDE Lin et al. (2025) , enable text- or depth-conditioned underwater scene synthesis. However, these methods focus on generating underwater scenes rather than modeling controllable degradations. Our work uniquely fills this gap by introducing a controllable, text-driven degradation diffusion model that synthesizes diverse and realistic underwater degradations, providing richer supervision and significantly enhancing the generalization of UIE models.

sections.heading: 3 Method
sections.text: Our methodology addresses the challenges of underwater image enhancement through a two-stage framework. First, to overcome the bottleneck of limited diversity and fixed degradation patterns in existing datasets, we introduce a Text-Conditioned Degradation Augmentation (TCDA) pipeline. This pipeline synthesizes a vast and diverse corpus of degraded images with controllable degradation attributes specified by fine-grained text prompts. Second, leveraging this augmented data, we employ a progressive degradation curriculum to train a Transmission-Guided One-Step Diffusion (TG-Diff) model, designed for transmission-guided image restoration with greater inference efficiency than multi-step diffusion methods.

sections.heading: 3.1 Text-Conditioned Degradation Augmentation
sections.text: As illustrated in Figure 2 , our TCDA pipeline establishes a controllable mapping between clean images, their degraded counterparts, and textual degradation prompts.

sections.heading: 3.1.1 Degradation Captioning via MLLMs
sections.text: We first collect a large-scale dataset of 12,483 degraded–clean image pairs from four representative underwater datasets: UIEB Li et al. (2019a) , EUVP Islam et al. (2020) , LSUI Peng et al. (2023) , and 3D TURBID Duarte et al. (2016) . To ensure fair evaluation, only the training subsets of UIEB and LSUI are used. To create rich, structured textual representations of the visual degradations, we employ a multimodal large language model (Gemini 2.5-Flash Team (2025) ) to generate fine-grained captions. These captions describe six core degradation attributes: turbidity level, color-cast type and severity, density of suspended particles, lighting conditions, degree of haze or backscatter, and extent of contrast reduction. To obtain more consistent captions, we guide the MLLM to describe degradation cues only, while excluding scene content. This process yields a dataset of triplets { I deg i , I clean i , T deg i } i = 1 N \{I^{i}_{\text{deg}},I^{i}_{\text{clean}},T^{i}_{\text{deg}}\}_{i=1}^{N} , where the text T deg i T^{i}_{\text{deg}} provides fine-grained supervision that directly links semantic attributes to visual degradation patterns, forming the foundation for our text-conditioned diffusion modeling. Details about the prompt design are provided in Supplementary Sec. 2.1. Figure 3: Overview of the proposed UIE framework. The model learns progressive degradation-aware enhancement through curriculum sampling and transmission-guided one-step diffusion, combining physical priors and text-conditioned cues for controllable restoration with greater inference efficiency than multi-step diffusion methods.

sections.heading: 3.1.2 Flow-Based Degradation Modeling
sections.text: Building upon the constructed triplets, we develop a text-conditioned diffusion framework to learn the mapping from clean to degraded representations. To model this directed transformation, we adopt a flow-based diffusion framework based on FLUX.1 Kontext Labs et al. (2025) . Unlike traditional denoising-based models, flow-matching directly learns the vector field from a source to a target distribution, offering a more stable and efficient training objective for this task. Specifically, the clean image I clean I_{\text{clean}} and degraded image I deg I_{\text{deg}} are encoded into compact latent representations x 0 x_{0} and x 1 x_{1} via a pre-trained VAE encoder. Concurrently, the textual description T deg T_{\text{deg}} is encoded by frozen dual text encoders (T5-XXL Raffel et al. (2020) and CLIP-L Radford et al. (2021) ) to obtain an embedding c c . The model learns a conditional velocity field v θ ​ ( z t , x 0 , t , c ) v_{\theta}(z_{t},x_{0},t,c) that drives the transformation of x 0 x_{0} towards x 1 x_{1} under text guidance. We adopt a flow-matching objective as ℒ degrade = 𝔼 t , x 0 , x 1 , c ​ [ ‖ v θ ​ ( z t , x 0 , t , c ) − ( ε − x 1 ) ‖ 2 2 ] , \mathcal{L}_{\text{degrade}}=\mathbb{E}_{t,x_{0},x_{1},c}\big[\|v_{\theta}(z_{t},x_{0},t,c)-(\varepsilon-x_{1})\|_{2}^{2}\big], (1) where z t z_{t} denotes the intermediate latent state at timestep t t , and ε ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , 1 ) \varepsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1) represents the stochastic noise. This formulation enables the model to learn a text-conditioned degradation vector field that reflects both the deterministic transformations described by the text and the stochastic variations inherent to real-world degradations. To enhance training efficiency and reduce computational overhead, we adopt parameter-efficient fine-tuning with LoRA Hu et al. (2022) .

sections.heading: 3.1.3 Controllable Degradation Synthesis
sections.text: To fully leverage our text-conditioned degradation model, we construct a structured prompt bank. Specifically, instead of relying on unconstrained free-form prompts, we organize the prompt space around six degradation attributes, including turbidity, color cast, particles, lighting, haze/backscatter, and contrast. For each attribute, we define phrases with different severity levels and group them into three difficulty tiers, i.e., easy, moderate, and hard, so that the resulting prompts are both semantically coherent and explicitly controllable. Each prompt is a tuple T deg = ( a 1 , … , a K , d ) T_{\text{deg}}=(a_{1},\ldots,a_{K},d) , detailing key attributes { a k } \{a_{k}\} and a difficulty level d ∈ { easy , moderate , hard } d\in\{\texttt{easy},\texttt{moderate},\texttt{hard}\} . During synthesis, given a clean image I clean I_{\text{clean}} and any such prompt T deg T_{\text{deg}} , our model generates a corresponding degraded image I deg I_{\text{deg}} . This text-driven paradigm not only enables fine-grained semantic control over degradation types and intensities but also provides the multi-difficulty data crucial for our progressive enhancement training, as detailed next. sections.heading: 3.2 Progressive Degradation Curriculum Learning
sections.text: Directly training a restoration model on the full, diverse spectrum of degradations generated by TCDA can lead to instability and slow convergence. To address this, we introduce a progressive degradation curriculum that leverages the difficulty levels defined in our prompt bank. This curriculum gradually increases the degradation complexity during training, allowing the model to first master fundamental color and tone restoration before tackling more complex scattering and contrast loss. sections.heading: 3.3 Transmission-Guided One-Step Diffusion
sections.text: To bridge the gap between physics-agnostic diffusion models and restoration with greater inference efficiency than multi-step diffusion methods, we propose Transmission-Guided One-Step Diffusion (TG-Diff). Our framework builds upon the single-step SD-Turbo architecture Sauer et al. (2024) , which we adapt to the UIE task. Runtime and model-complexity comparisons are provided in Supplementary Sec. 3.1. We freeze the pre-trained weights and apply LoRA Hu et al. (2022) with a rank of 32 to both the U-Net and the VAE encoder. To provide the diffusion model with a dense spatial prior on attenuation and scattering, we condition it on a transmission map 𝒯 \mathcal{T} estimated via the UDCP method Drews et al. (2013) . This strategy provides the model with a physics-inspired cue about spatially varying water properties. To achieve this, the map is downsampled to the latent resolution and concatenated with the image latent z deg z_{\text{deg}} , forming an expanded 5-channel input x = [ z deg , 𝒯 latent ] x=[z_{\text{deg}},\mathcal{T}_{\text{latent}}] where new channel weights are zero-initialized. Furthermore, to preserve high-frequency details during the single-step process, we augment the VAE with multi-scale skip connections. In this process, an intermediate skip feature S i S_{i} is first generated from the encoder feature E i E_{i} via a 1 × 1 1\times 1 convolution. This feature is then added to the corresponding upsampled decoder feature U i U_{i} as: S i = Conv 1 × 1 ​ ( E i ) , U i ← Interp ​ ( U i ) + S i . sections.heading: 4.1 Experimental Setup
sections.text: Implementation Details. In the TCDA pipeline, we utilize two NVIDIA A800 GPUs (80 GB) for training the degradation diffusion model. We adopt a LoRA fine-tuning strategy with a rank of 8. All the images are resized to 1024×1024 in the training process. The model is optimized using AdamW with a learning rate of 1 × 10 − 4 1\times 10^{-4} and a per-GPU batch size of 1. We train the model for two epochs. During inference, we employ 28 denoising steps for text-conditioned degradation synthesis. For training the TG-Diff, we adopt the Stable Diffusion-Turbo Sauer et al. (2024) as our base model and fine-tune it with LoRA of rank 32. During the training process, the samples are randomly cropped into 256 × \times 256 patches from the original images. We train the model for 50,000 iterations using the AdamW optimizer ( β 1 = 0.9 , β 2 = 0.999 \beta_{1}=0.9,\beta_{2}=0.999 ) with a constant learning rate of 1 × 10 − 4 1\times 10^{-4} and a batch size of 12 per GPU. We optimize TG-Diff with the composite objective ℒ total = ℒ L1 + α ​ ℒ LPIPS \mathcal{L}_{\text{total}}=\mathcal{L}_{\text{L1}}+\alpha\,\mathcal{L}_{\text{LPIPS}} , which combines the L1 reconstruction loss ( ℒ L1 \mathcal{L}_{\text{L1}} ) and the LPIPS perceptual loss ( ℒ LPIPS \mathcal{L}_{\text{LPIPS}} ), with α = 3.3 \alpha=3.3 in all experiments. Datasets and Evaluation Metrics. All images in the UIEB dataset Li et al. (2019a) are first divided into 790 images for training and 100 images for testing. Based on 790 training images, we further utilize our text-conditioned degradation augmentation (TCDA) model to produce 10,270 augmented images. These augmented images are categorized into three difficulty levels (easy, moderate, and hard) with a ratio of 5:5:3. To assess the benefit of TCDA, we train all underwater image enhancement models with and without 10,270 augmented images, and then evaluate them on the same UIEB test set. For paired evaluations, we report PSNR Huynh-Thu and Ghanbari (2008) , SSIM Wang et al. (2004) , and LPIPS Zhang et al. (2018) to measure reconstruction fidelity. For unpaired evaluations, we employ two no-reference underwater quality metrics: UCIQE Yang and Sowmya (2015) and UIQM Panetta et al. (2015) . In addition, we assess performance on the reference-free UIEB C60 subset Li et al. (2019a) and U45 dataset Li et al. (2019b) , using UCIQE and UIQM to measure enhancement quality under unpaired conditions.

sections.heading: 4.2 Comparison with State-of-the-Arts
sections.text: We compare our approach with several state-of-the-art UIE methods, including UIEC 2 -Net Wang et al. (2021) , SCNet Fu et al. (2022) , FiveA+ Jiang et al. (2023) , WF-Diff Zhao et al. (2024) , CE-VAE Pucci and Martinel (2025) , and Phaseformer Khan et al. (2025) . Quantitative Evaluation. The quantitative comparisons in Table 1 show that our method achieves the strongest overall performance across three underwater benchmarks. On the paired UIEB dataset, TG-Diff further achieves the best SSIM (0.927), PSNR (22.341), LPIPS (0.129), and UCIQE (0.613) after applying TCDA. On the reference-free C60 and U45 benchmarks, our method also obtains the highest UCIQE and UIQM scores in most cases, indicating improved performance on these reference-free metrics. TCDA improves most reported metrics across the compared methods. A discussion of occasional UIQM decreases is provided in Supplementary Sec. 3.2. Qualitative Evaluation. Figure 5 presents visual comparisons on representative UIEB examples with different degradation levels. Existing methods often suffer from distinct artifacts: UIEC 2 -Net tends to leave residual haze and muted colors, SCNet and FiveA+ may introduce over-enhancement or unnatural color shifts, WF-Diff and CE-VAE sometimes fail to fully recover fine structures, and Phaseformer, although stronger, still shows less stable restoration under severe degradations. In contrast, our TG-Diff produces clearer visibility, more natural color balance, and better local detail recovery, as highlighted in the enlarged regions. After incorporating TCDA, “Ours+TCDA” further improves restoration fidelity, especially in heavily degraded scenes, where it removes haze more thoroughly and recovers clearer textures and structures. These results verify that the proposed data-centric curriculum not only improves objective performance but also leads to more visually reliable enhancement results. sections.heading: 4.3 Ablation Studies
sections.text: Effectiveness of Transmission-Guided One-Step Diffusion. We investigate each TG-Diff component through the quantitative and qualitative results in Table 2 and Figure 6 . Starting from the single-step backbone, making the encoder trainable improves feature adaptability, while adding skip connections further enhances structural fidelity. Incorporating the UDCP prior improves SSIM and LPIPS while maintaining comparable PSNR, indicating complementary benefits from the transmission cue. sections.heading: 5 Conclusion
sections.text: In this work, we propose an explicit, controllable degradation modeling framework designed to alleviate the scale and diversity limitations of paired UIE data. We introduce TCDA to synthesize diverse underwater degradations with fine-grained textual control, a progressive degradation curriculum to organize these samples across attributes and difficulty levels, and TG-Diff to incorporate a transmission prior into one-step restoration. Together, these components convert controllable degradation modeling into structured supervision for robust UIE. Experiments on multiple benchmarks demonstrate improvements across most restoration and reference-free metrics, while the ablation studies examine the contributions of the curriculum, data augmentation, and transmission guidance. Future work will extend the framework to temporally consistent underwater video enhancement and broader real-world degradation conditions. Data Availability Statement. In this work, we generate augmented training data for underwater image enhancement. The data is available in: https://github.com/ANTIT-Pixel/Rethinking-Underwater-Image-Enhancement . Acknowledgment. Such scarce and insufficient data ultimately restrict the generalization of underwater image enhancement models, highlighting the need for realistic and controllable degradation modeling to better capture real underwater conditions and improve enhancement robustness. To this end, we propose a unified degradation-aware training framework for the underwater image enhancement task. A Text-Conditioned Degradation Augmentation Pipeline uses a text-guided diffusion model to synthesize diverse and semantically consistent degraded samples, providing paired data to support the subsequent curriculum learning strategy. The proposed Progressive Degradation Curriculum organizes training across multiple attributes and difficulty levels to promote balanced learning, and a Transmission-Guided One-Step Diffusion Model leverages this progressive process to better address the wide range of degradation severity and restoration ambiguity in underwater images. Extensive experiments on multiple underwater benchmarks demonstrate that our proposed method achieves superior performance. Figure 1: Top : Illustration of three common routes for constructing paired underwater datasets. Medium : Proposed text-driven degradation diffusion paradigm for controllable underwater degradation synthesis. Bottom : Quantitative results of our method on performance improvement and synthesis quality. 1 Introduction Underwater Image Enhancement (UIE) aims to recover clear, color-consistent, and detail-preserving images from degraded underwater observations. Unlike uniform degradations in common image restoration tasks, underwater degradations are highly heterogeneous and scene-dependent, where they vary with water type, depth, illumination, and particle density, and often exhibit complex spatial coupling among these factors. Consequently, the underlying degradation distribution is extremely difficult to model or approximate with a fixed prior, making UIE an intrinsically ill-posed and data-sensitive problem. Over the past decade, a wide range of enhancement approaches have been explored, spanning from physics-based restoration guided by analytical priors Drews et al. (2013) ; Galdran et al. (2015) ; Chiang and Chen (2011) to deep learning-based methods trained on paired datasets Li et al. (2020) ; Li et al. (2021) ; Wang et al. (2021) ; Zhang et al. (2022) ; Wei et al. (2022) ; Li et al. (2019a) . While the former provides physical interpretability, it fails to generalize across diverse water types and illumination conditions. The latter achieves stronger visual quality through elaborately designed networks but relies heavily on limited paired data. Acquiring paired underwater data is inherently challenging because capturing the same scene under both degraded and clean conditions is almost impossible in dynamic environments. As illustrated in Figure 1 -Top, such pairs are commonly obtained through (i) controlled water-tank capture Duarte et al. (2016) , (ii) pseudo-reference generation by manually selecting outputs from multiple UIE methods Li et al. (2019a) ; Peng et al. (2023) , or (iii) synthetic rendering with simplified underwater formation models Islam et al. (2020) ; Li et al. (2017) ; Ye et al. (2022) ; Li et al. (2020) . The first two routes provide visually realistic supervision but are costly and difficult to scale, whereas the third enables scalable generation but often fails to reproduce the complex lighting and scattering effects of natural underwater scenes. These limitations reveal that the main bottleneck of UIE lies not only in model architecture but also in the lack of realistic and controllable degradation modeling for generating diverse training variants. Moreover, underwater degradations vary drastically in strength and composition—ranging from light color cast to dense scattering and mixed turbidity. This motivates us to rethink UIE — not as direct restoration, but as learning from degradation , where controllable, text-guided degradation modeling provides structured, degradation-aware supervision for enhancement learning. In addition, we argue that if degradations can be explicitly modeled and controlled, they can serve as a meaningful curriculum for enhancement, where the model gradually adapts to increasingly challenging degradations across multiple attributes and severity levels, which encourages more generalized enhancement performance. To this end, we revisit underwater enhancement from a new perspective-leveraging the generative capability of the diffusion model to explicitly model and control underwater degradations (Figure 1 -Medium). Diffusion-based generative models Labs et al. (2025) provide an expressive latent space in which degradations can be synthesized and conditioned on semantic cues such as turbidity, illumination, or particle density. This text-conditioned formulation enables fine-grained control over degradation attributes and supports large-scale data augmentation aligned with real underwater characteristics. The generated degradations further provide difficulty-aware cues that guide enhancement models to learn progressively under well-structured degradation distributions, yielding more stable optimization and visually coherent restoration across diverse underwater conditions. Moreover, we develop a Transmission-Guided One-Step Diffusion enhancer that injects a transmission prior into the latent space and performs a single deterministic reverse update, providing transmission-guided restoration with lower sampling cost than multi-step diffusion methods. Together, these designs establish a cohesive paradigm that unifies controllable degradation modeling and physically guided enhancement, offering a new perspective on the UIE task. Overall, our contributions can be summarized as follows: • We introduce a Text-Conditioned Degradation Augmentation (TCDA) pipeline that leverages a text-guided diffusion model to synthesize controllable degraded variants of clean images, enabling fine-grained attribute/severity control for task-aligned data augmentation. • We employ a progressive degradation curriculum learning that gradually increases training difficulty, stabilizing optimization and improving the model’s robustness. • We design a Transmission-Guided One-step Diffusion model (TG-Diff) that embeds a transmission prior into the latent space, achieving high-quality restoration with greater inference efficiency than multi-step diffusion methods. • Extensive experiments on multiple underwater benchmarks demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance. Figure 2: Overview of the proposed Text-Conditioned Degradation Augmentation (TCDA) pipeline. It consists of four stages: (1) Degradation Captioning via MLLMs for generating fine-grained textual descriptions of underwater degradations, (2) Flow-Based Degradation Modeling for learning text-conditioned mappings between clean and degraded representations, (3) Prompt-Space Augmentation for enriching degradation prompts with varying difficulty levels, and (4) Text-Conditioned Degradation Synthesis for controllable degradation generation to support curriculum learning. 2 Related Work 2.1 Underwater Image Enhancement Traditional UIE methods are typically built upon the underwater image formation model that characterizes light scattering and absorption. Early works such as underwater dark channel prior Drews et al. (2013) , red channel prior Galdran et al. (2015) , and blurriness-based estimation Chiang and Chen (2011) estimate the transmission map and background light to remove haze and recover true colors. More recent prior-based methods further exploit illumination characteristics to handle non-uniform lighting and color degradation Hou et al. (2023) ; Zhou et al. (2025b) . However, their performance heavily depends on accurate estimation of water parameters and scene depth, limiting their robustness across varying underwater conditions Liu et al. (2020) . Deep learning has revolutionized UIE by providing strong nonlinear modeling and robust feature representation capabilities. Early convolutional methods Li et al. (2020) ; Li et al. (2021) ; Wang et al. (2021) ; Zhang et al. (2022) ; Wei et al. (2022) employed encoder–decoder or multi-branch architectures to learn direct mappings from degraded to clean images, achieving improved contrast and color fidelity through illumination modeling and multi-level feature learning. Adversarial and generative frameworks Fabbri et al. (2018) ; Wang et al. (2019) further enhanced perceptual realism but often introduced instability and color over-saturation. Moreover, some works use contrastive learning Zhou et al. (2024) , domain priors, and external knowledge to improve UIE generalization and controllability. PhaseFormer Khan et al. (2025) introduces phase-based attention to preserve structural cues, while CLIP-UIE Liu et al. (2025) utilizes semantic guidance from vision-language models. Semantic-Guided Diffusion Zhou et al. (2025a) leverages multimodal cues from LLaVA and Zip-CLIP to generate semantic heatmaps for diffusion guidance. Recent studies highlight the role of generative priors and degradation modeling in diffusion-based image restoration Li et al. (2025) . Underwater-specific approaches, including WF-Diff Zhao et al. (2024) and SLURPP Wu et al. (2025) , exploit diffusion models for underwater enhancement. Related diffusion-based restoration methods further explore degradation-model optimization Fei et al. (2026) , global brightness alignment Guo et al. (2026) , and blur-decoupled learning Cheng et al. (2026) . Despite these advances, the effectiveness of related UIE methods remains largely constrained by the availability and diversity of training data. 2.2 Underwater Image Synthesis The scarcity of paired and diverse underwater data has motivated the research on underwater image synthesis. Early physics-based methods simulate light attenuation using simplified water models but fail to reproduce complex scattering Ye et al. (2022) ; Li et al. (2020) . Alternatively, some datasets create pseudo-references by applying multiple UIE methods to a degraded image and having a user select the best outcome as the “clean” target Li et al. (2019a) . While visually plausible, this approach is fundamentally limited as it provides no insight into the forward degradation process itself. It merely offers a single, fixed enhancement target for each input, failing to model the diverse and controllable degradation attributes (e.g., water type, turbidity) that are crucial for robust generalization. GAN-based approaches Li et al. (2017) ; Islam et al. (2020) improve realism but suffer from domain bias and unstable training. Recent diffusion-driven frameworks, including Atlantis++ Zhang et al. (2026) and TIDE Lin et al. (2025) , enable text- or depth-conditioned underwater scene synthesis. However, these methods focus on generating underwater scenes rather than modeling controllable degradations. Our work uniquely fills this gap by introducing a controllable, text-driven degradation diffusion model that synthesizes diverse and realistic underwater degradations, providing richer supervision and significantly enhancing the generalization of UIE models. 3 Method Our methodology addresses the challenges of underwater image enhancement through a two-stage framework. First, to overcome the bottleneck of limited diversity and fixed degradation patterns in existing datasets, we introduce a Text-Conditioned Degradation Augmentation (TCDA) pipeline. This pipeline synthesizes a vast and diverse corpus of degraded images with controllable degradation attributes specified by fine-grained text prompts. Second, leveraging this augmented data, we employ a progressive degradation curriculum to train a Transmission-Guided One-Step Diffusion (TG-Diff) model, designed for transmission-guided image restoration with greater inference efficiency than multi-step diffusion methods. 3.1 Text-Conditioned Degradation Augmentation As illustrated in Figure 2 , our TCDA pipeline establishes a controllable mapping between clean images, their degraded counterparts, and textual degradation prompts. 3.1.1 Degradation Captioning via MLLMs We first collect a large-scale dataset of 12,483 degraded–clean image pairs from four representative underwater datasets: UIEB Li et al. (2019a) , EUVP Islam et al. (2020) , LSUI Peng et al. (2023) , and 3D TURBID Duarte et al. (2016) . To ensure fair evaluation, only the training subsets of UIEB and LSUI are used. To create rich, structured textual representations of the visual degradations, we employ a multimodal large language model (Gemini 2.5-Flash Team (2025) ) to generate fine-grained captions. These captions describe six core degradation attributes: turbidity level, color-cast type and severity, density of suspended particles, lighting conditions, degree of haze or backscatter, and extent of contrast reduction. To obtain more consistent captions, we guide the MLLM to describe degradation cues only, while excluding scene content. This process yields a dataset of triplets { I deg i , I clean i , T deg i } i = 1 N \{I^{i}_{\text{deg}},I^{i}_{\text{clean}},T^{i}_{\text{deg}}\}_{i=1}^{N} , where the text T deg i T^{i}_{\text{deg}} provides fine-grained supervision that directly links semantic attributes to visual degradation patterns, forming the foundation for our text-conditioned diffusion modeling. Specifically, instead of relying on unconstrained free-form prompts, we organize the prompt space around six degradation attributes, including turbidity, color cast, particles, lighting, haze/backscatter, and contrast. For each attribute, we define phrases with different severity levels and group them into three difficulty tiers, i.e., easy, moderate, and hard, so that the resulting prompts are both semantically coherent and explicitly controllable. Our framework builds upon the single-step SD-Turbo architecture Sauer et al. (2024) , which we adapt to the UIE task. Runtime and model-complexity comparisons are provided in Supplementary Sec. 3.1. We freeze the pre-trained weights and apply LoRA Hu et al. (2022) with a rank of 32 to both the U-Net and the VAE encoder. To provide the diffusion model with a dense spatial prior on attenuation and scattering, we condition it on a transmission map 𝒯 \mathcal{T} estimated via the UDCP method Drews et al. (2013) . This strategy provides the model with a physics-inspired cue about spatially varying water properties. To achieve this, the map is downsampled to the latent resolution and concatenated with the image latent z deg z_{\text{deg}} , forming an expanded 5-channel input x = [ z deg , 𝒯 latent ] x=[z_{\text{deg}},\mathcal{T}_{\text{latent}}] where new channel weights are zero-initialized. Furthermore, to preserve high-frequency details during the single-step process, we augment the VAE with multi-scale skip connections. In this process, an intermediate skip feature S i S_{i} is first generated from the encoder feature E i E_{i} via a 1 × 1 1\times 1 convolution. Figure 5 presents visual comparisons on representative UIEB examples with different degradation levels. Existing methods often suffer from distinct artifacts: UIEC 2 -Net tends to leave residual haze and muted colors, SCNet and FiveA+ may introduce over-enhancement or unnatural color shifts, WF-Diff and CE-VAE sometimes fail to fully recover fine structures, and Phaseformer, although stronger, still shows less stable restoration under severe degradations. Both UCIQE and UIQM consistently decrease as the degradation difficulty increases from easy to hard. 5 Conclusion In this work, we propose an explicit, controllable degradation modeling framework designed to alleviate the scale and diversity limitations of paired UIE data. We introduce TCDA to synthesize diverse underwater degradations with fine-grained textual control, a progressive degradation curriculum to organize these samples across attributes and difficulty levels, and TG-Diff to incorporate a transmission prior into one-step restoration. Together, these components convert controllable degradation modeling into structured supervision for robust UIE. Experiments on multiple benchmarks demonstrate improvements across most restoration and reference-free metrics, while the ablation studies examine the contributions of the curriculum, data augmentation, and transmission guidance. Future work will extend the framework to temporally consistent underwater video enhancement and broader real-world degradation conditions. Data Availability Statement.
